clue.text: Said to include part like m25?

indicators.note: to include tells you the word for said takes the word for part inside it

parts.note: said, as an adjective, means spoken or oral
a bit is a small part of something

explanation.surface: Something spoken is meant to cover a section resembling London's ring road.
explanation.walkthrough: The M25 is the motorway that circles London; the question mark admits it is just one example of such a road.
explanation.definitionFit: The M25 loops right round London, so it is an example of a ring road circling a city.

clue.text: Huge houses work? I'm wrong

indicators.note: houses says the word for huge gives the word for work a home inside it

parts.note: OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize, very large
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Does an enormous building hold a workplace? The speaker admits a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation uttered on realising you have made a mistake.

clue.text: No fun being carried

definitions.meaning: as a noun, a tedious person or thing that gives no enjoyment
the past tense of bear, to carry or transport

explanation.surface: Being given a lift turns out to be dull.
explanation.definitionFit: A tedious thing gives no enjoyment, and the same spelling is the past tense of bear, meaning transported.

clue.text: Hairy hen, term for giant hangover

indicators.note: hairy can mean wild or scary, so the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shaggy chicken is slang for an enormous headache from drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' is the anagram signal: the fifteen letters of HEN, TERM, FOR and GIANT are rearranged. 'term for' looks like a link but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the day following heavy drinking, when the unpleasant effects are felt.

clue.text: A river with new crossing? I'm honoured

indicators.note: crossing says the word for new spans the A and the river, sitting on both sides of them

parts.note: late can mean recent, as in the late news or 'of late'
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire, England

explanation.surface: A waterway has a fresh bridge, and the speaker has been given the privilege of opening it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone crowned with an award, like a Nobel prizewinner or official poet, speaks here in the first person.

clue.text: College party — left after one round

indicators.note: after places the letter for left following the letters for one and round

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance party
I is the Roman numeral for one
O is the round letter

explanation.surface: At a student bash, someone departed once a single set of drinks was finished.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: one of the oldest constituent foundations of Oxford University.

clue.text: Potion is northern broth

parts.note: a brew is a concocted drink, such as a witch's potion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A magic drink turns out to be a soup from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like a link word but supplies the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect word from the north of England for a soup, or bread soaked in it.

clue.text: Easy reading, I agree, till truth comes out

indicators.note: comes out suggests the letters emerge in a different form from the one printed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The speaker concedes a book is undemanding, until its real message emerges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes out' is the anagram signal: the fifteen letters of I, AGREE, TILL and TRUTH are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Books that are undemanding and entertaining, picked up for pleasure rather than study.

clue.text: Is it OK for me to turn clergyman out?

indicators.note: to turn tells you the two-word question before it is written backwards

parts.note: 'Can I?' is how you ask whether something is OK for you to do
a curate is a junior Anglican cleric who assists a parish priest

explanation.surface: Someone asks permission to evict a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' flips CANI to INAC. 'out' looks like part of evicting the clergyman, but it is the definition, as in sums being out.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure that is out is off the mark, as in 'my sums were out by ten'.

clue.text: Joe and what he was — a real bargain

parts.note: Joe Loss ran a hugely popular British dance orchestra from the 1930s onwards
the man fronted a dance band, so he was its leader

explanation.surface: A man called Joe and his former occupation add up to a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Loss fronted one of Britain's best-known dance bands from the 1930s to the 1980s; his surname and his job spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An item sold below cost to draw shoppers in, so a genuine cut-price buy for the customer.

clue.text: Hound by itself, adorable

parts.note: per se is the Latin phrase meaning by or in itself
cute means sweet and adorable

explanation.surface: A dog on its own, looking sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hound' reads as a noun, the dog; it is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, a synonym: to harass or pursue someone relentlessly.

clue.text: Perhaps bent copper may rely on him?

definitions.meaning: bent is a stiff, wiry plant of lawns and pastures, one example of the family
in British slang, an informer who tells the police about fellow criminals

explanation.surface: A corrupt police officer might depend on a certain man.
explanation.definitionFit: Bent is one variety of the lawn plant, and in British slang the word also means a police informer.

clue.text: Technical term for "booby"?

parts.note: booby is read whimsically as boob-y, full of boobs or blunders; the learned adjective for containing a blunder of grammar or manners is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: A solecism is a blunder in grammar or etiquette, so its formal adjective fits something jokingly called boob-y.

clue.text: Energy — I'm in place to make a guess

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

indicators.note: in puts the letters of I'm inside the word for place

parts.note: to station someone is to place them, and a station is a post or place
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Full of vigour, the speaker is in position to hazard an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough calculation or judgement of size or value, a synonym for an informed stab.

clue.text: Health & safety call about papa's tumble

indicators.note: about says the abbreviation and the word for call together go round the letter for papa

parts.note: abbreviated to H & S, with the ampersand spelt out as 'and'
to ring someone is to call them by phone
Papa is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for P

explanation.surface: A workplace-safety phone report concerning Dad's fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnastic move in which you flip over via your palms, an example of an acrobatic roll or flip.

clue.text: Half of country hampered by present decline

indicators.note: hampered by pictures the half-word hemmed in on both sides by the word for present

parts.note: to present a show is to stage it

indicators.note: half of takes the first three of the six letters of the word for country

parts.note: a nation is a country

explanation.surface: Part of the nation is held back by the current slump.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop developing and go stale is to fall away, a loose synonym.

clue.text: Chain that Romeo is not after

definitions.meaning: a long range of jagged mountains, as in Spain or the Americas
in the NATO phonetic alphabet Romeo (R) comes just before the word for S, never following it

explanation.surface: A piece of jewellery that the famous lover isn't pursuing.
explanation.definitionFit: A jagged mountain range is a line of peaks, and the same word follows Romeo in the NATO spelling alphabet.

clue.text: Glass bottle may be in this bin as I do juggling

definitions.text: Glass bottle may be in this

indicators.note: juggling tosses things around, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A glass bottle might end up in this recycling container while the speaker performs a juggling act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'juggling' is the anagram signal for BIN AS I DO. 'this bin' seems to hold the bottle, but the definition stops at 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark natural volcanic glass, resembling bottle-glass, from which vessels have been carved since antiquity.

clue.text: I shout about lunch?

indicators.note: about turns the shout round, so it is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: oi is a shout to get someone's attention
to lunch is to dine, the question mark admitting it is only one example of a meal

explanation.surface: The speaker yells that it's time for the midday meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'I' is not the speaker but a chemical symbol, and the whole definition; 'about' turns OI into IO.
explanation.definitionFit: I is the chemical symbol for this element, a halogen used as an antiseptic.

clue.text: Bunker is a mountain around second tee

indicators.note: around puts the word for mountain on either side of the letter for second

parts.note: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis
taken as written

explanation.surface: A golf course's sand trap is a hill surrounding the tee at the second hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunker' looks like the golf hazard; here it is one who bunks off, British slang for skipping school or work.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to bunk off is to skip school or work, so a bunker is whimsically someone who stays away.

clue.text: Old country, a country that was unfinished

parts.note: per means a, as in fifty pence a (per) pound

indicators.note: unfinished says the former country's name stops short, losing its final letter

parts.note: Siam is the former name of Thailand, so a country that was

explanation.surface: An ancient state, one that was never completed.
explanation.walkthrough: The little 'a' is not a link: it gives PER. 'unfinished' cuts SIAM to SIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The historical name for Iran, used in the West until 1935.

clue.text: How first letters appear, for example

definitions.text: How first letters appear, for example

parts.words: How first letters appear, for example
parts.note: the letters of the word 'first' itself, f-i-r-s-t, happen to run in A-to-Z order, making that word one example

explanation.walkthrough: Not initials: read 'first letters' as the letters of the word 'first', which happen to run in A-to-Z order.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters f, i, r, s, t of the word 'first' come in dictionary order, so that word is one instance.

clue.text: "Am I bovvered?", Lauren's first communication

indicators.note: bovvered is 'bothered' in a London accent, and bothered letters are disturbed out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the name Lauren's

explanation.surface: A stroppy teenager's catchphrase is the opening thing Lauren ever says.
explanation.walkthrough: Lauren is British comedian Catherine Tate's teenage character, whose catchphrase is 'Am I bovvered?'; 'bovvered' swaps the two letters of the opening word.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters and messages sent by post or electronically are one form of this.

clue.text: Boss sees work unfinished

indicators.note: unfinished says the word for work stops short, losing its last letter

parts.note: to study is to work at a subject, and a study is a piece of work

explanation.surface: The manager notices a job left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is not a manager but a raised knob, as on a shield; 'unfinished' cuts STUDY short.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a raised knob or ornamental projection on a surface such as a shield.

clue.text: Username one changed to "bonehead"

parts.note: your ID is the name you log in with
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: changed says the two letters of the word after it swap places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's login name was altered to an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed to' reads as a plain phrase, but 'changed' rearranges TO into OT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are insults for a stupid person.

clue.text: Reduced temperature in putting on pepper

indicators.note: in places the letter for temperature inside the word for putting on

parts.note: to put on is to feign, and simulant is an adjective meaning feigning or simulating

indicators.note: reduced cuts temperature down to its standard one-letter abbreviation, its opening letter

explanation.surface: A lower heat while adding the seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' shrinks temperature to T, and 'in' puts it inside SIMULANT, an adjective meaning feigning.
explanation.definitionFit: The pungent spice is classed as something that rouses appetite and digestion, so it is an example.

clue.text: Rejected song for one home nation

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the three pieces together are read from the end to the start

parts.note: an air is a tune or song
for one means for example, abbreviated e.g.
in means at home

explanation.surface: A tune turned down as the anthem for one of the UK's countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' turns all three pieces as one run, last piece first. 'home nation' (a country of the UK) is split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A West African country, the most populous on the continent, so one example.

clue.text: Was annoyance driven by desire?

indicators.note: by sets the word for driven next to the word for desire, as in a hyphenated phrase like demand-led

parts.note: a need is a want or desire
led means steered or driven, as in market-led

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone's irritation was caused by wanting something.
explanation.definitionFit: To irritate or provoke someone, in the past tense, is loosely to have been an irritation to them.
